explanations.explanation: That's the name Elisha gives, friend. He says to look for "Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi" (2 Kings 9:2). Elisha even gives the family tree, so the young man can't grab the wrong commander. When your errand involves a flask of oil, you want the right head.

Joab was a commander too, one who served under David (2 Samuel 8:16), so I see how he came to mind. But Elisha never says his name. He sends the young man to look for Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi (2 Kings 9:2). Joab belongs to an earlier chapter of Israel's story.

Abner was the commander of Saul's army (1 Samuel 14:50), so he's a fair guess for a soldier's name. Elisha doesn't send the young man to him, though. The one to look for is Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi (2 Kings 9:2). Same job as Abner, but a whole different man.

Yep, Elisha says to "get him away from his companions, and take him to an inner room" (2 Kings 9:2). The message is for Jehu and nobody else at the table. I'd say that room is as private as it gets. Not a word of this gets out until the door closes.

A city gate is about the busiest, most public spot there is, so it's the opposite of what Elisha says. He tells the young man to take Jehu to an inner room (2 Kings 9:2). First Jehu gets pulled away from his companions, then he's brought somewhere private. Nobody pours oil on a head in front of a crowd on this errand.

The army commanders are already sitting together when the young prophet arrives (2 Kings 9:5), so he's right in the middle of the army. But Elisha's plan is the reverse of that. He says to get Jehu away from his companions and take him to an inner room (2 Kings 9:2). A camp full of soldiers is the very crowd he's supposed to leave behind.
King it is. The words Elisha gives him are: "I anoint you king over Israel" (2 Kings 9:3). In the Dorinverse, that is a LOT of news for one flask of oil. And Jehu didn't see a bit of it coming.

Judges were leaders in Israel long before this, but that isn't the word here. Elisha tells the young prophet to say, "I anoint you king over Israel" (2 Kings 9:3). Jehu is getting the whole crown, friend, not a smaller seat.

Oil was used on priests in Israel too, so I see why that one tempts people (Exodus 30:30). But Elisha's words are different: "I anoint you king over Israel" (2 Kings 9:3). Same oil, but the title poured out here is king.
Staying isn't in the plan at all. After the anointing, Elisha says, "Then open the door and run. Do not delay!" (2 Kings 9:3). There's no waiting around for an answer. Say it, pour it, and RUN.

That's right, there's no waiting. Elisha says, "Then open the door and run. Do not delay!" (2 Kings 9:3). The young prophet's job is to deliver the LORD's word and go. Not one extra minute in that room, friend.

Yes. The young prophet says, "I have a message for you, commander," and Jehu asks, "For which of us?" (2 Kings 9:5). Think about it, a whole table of commanders and every one of them wonders if it's him. The young man answers, "For you, commander," and that settles it.

Jehu does ask. When the young prophet says he has a message for the commander, Jehu answers, "For which of us?" (2 Kings 9:5). With a table full of commanders, I'd ask too. The young prophet says, "For you, commander," and Jehu gets up.

That's the one. The LORD says, "you are to strike down the house of your master Ahab" (2 Kings 9:7). Ahab was king of Israel before his son Joram. Jehu has been serving under that house, and now the LORD hands him this job.

Saul was an earlier king of Israel (1 Samuel 11:15), so the guess isn't random. But the LORD never names Saul's house here. He tells Jehu to strike down the house of "your master Ahab" (2 Kings 9:7). The house in question is the one Jehu has been serving.

Hazael is the king of Aram, the one Joram was fighting at Ramoth-gilead (2 Kings 8:28-29). He's in the neighborhood of this story, so I see the pull. But the LORD points Jehu at a different house. He says, "you are to strike down the house of your master Ahab" (2 Kings 9:7).

explanations.answer: To avenge the blood of His prophets
explanations.explanation: Right. The LORD says it is "so that I may avenge the blood of My servants the prophets and the blood of all the servants of the LORD shed by the hand of Jezebel" (2 Kings 9:7). Notice the LORD gives the reason Himself, so we don't have to guess. Those servants were not forgotten.

explanations.answer: To return the throne to David's family
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a tidy ending, but the LORD doesn't say it here. His reason is "so that I may avenge the blood of My servants the prophets and the blood of all the servants of the LORD" (2 Kings 9:7). And the anointing is over Israel, with Jehu as the king. David's family doesn't come up in these words.

explanations.answer: To make room for a new temple
explanations.explanation: No temple plans anywhere in this message, friend. The reason the LORD gives is that He will "avenge the blood of My servants the prophets and the blood of all the servants of the LORD shed by the hand of Jezebel" (2 Kings 9:7). Jezebel is Ahab's wife, and her name is tied to that blood.

It's the other way around. The LORD says the dogs will devour Jezebel on the plot of ground at Jezreel, and "there will be no one to bury her" (2 Kings 9:10). This is a heavy part of the message. I think we can just let it be heavy.
Right, no burial. The LORD says, "…there will be no one to bury her." (2 Kings 9:10). It comes with the dogs devouring Jezebel at Jezreel. That's a hard word, and I think it's fine to say so.

That's the word they use. They ask, "Is everything all right? Why did this madman come to you?" (2 Kings 9:11). They saw a young man dash in and dash out, and that was their read. I've been called worse by a stack of takeout menus.

A spy would at least have been sneaking, and I see why that came to mind. But the servants never say that word. They ask, "Why did this madman come to you?" (2 Kings 9:11). They saw a man who didn't act like a normal visitor.

A beggar would have hung around to ask for something, wouldn't he? This young man did the opposite and ran. The servants ask, "Why did this madman come to you?" (2 Kings 9:11). They call him a madman, not a beggar.

explanations.answer: He brushes it off as prophet babble
explanations.explanation: That's how he starts. Jehu says, "You know his kind and their babble" (2 Kings 9:11). He makes it sound like nothing, the way you'd wave off a group chat that got loud. It doesn't hold up for long.

explanations.answer: He says the man had the wrong commander
explanations.explanation: That isn't Jehu's answer. The young prophet said plainly, "For you, commander" (2 Kings 9:5), and Jehu had gone in with him. What Jehu tells the servants is, "You know his kind and their babble" (2 Kings 9:11). He waves it off instead of saying it was a mix-up.

explanations.answer: He says the man came asking for money
explanations.explanation: Money never comes up. Jehu's first answer is, "You know his kind and their babble" (2 Kings 9:11). He's brushing off the visit, not making up a reason for it. He plays it down like it was nothing.

explanations.answer: The LORD anointed him king over Israel
explanations.explanation: Right. Jehu says the man talked about "this and that," and then repeats the words: "This is what the LORD says: I anoint you king over Israel" (2 Kings 9:12). The servants pushed, and out came the big news. I'd have cracked by the second "Tell us now!" myself.

explanations.answer: The prophet brought news of a battle
explanations.explanation: Battles are in the air at Ramoth-gilead, so it's an understandable guess. But that isn't what Jehu says. He tells them the man spoke of "this and that," saying, "This is what the LORD says: I anoint you king over Israel" (2 Kings 9:12).

explanations.answer: Elisha wants to meet with him soon
explanations.explanation: Elisha sent the young prophet, but Jehu never says anything about a meeting. When the servants push him, he repeats the message: "This is what the LORD says: I anoint you king over Israel" (2 Kings 9:12). The news is about a crown, not a meeting.

Yes, each man takes his garment and puts it under Jehu on the bare steps (2 Kings 9:13). They do it quickly, with no speeches first. Nobody went looking for a rug, they just used what they were wearing.

These are soldiers, so a shield isn't a crazy guess. But the text says each man took his garment. They put it under Jehu on the bare steps (2 Kings 9:13). A shield wouldn't make much of a carpet, friend.

Swords would make a rough welcome mat, wouldn't they? The text says each man took his garment and put it under Jehu on the bare steps (2 Kings 9:13). Nobody lays down a weapon here. They lay down their clothes.
They sure do. They blow the ram's horn and proclaim, "Jehu is king!" (2 Kings 9:13). A few minutes ago he was sitting with the commanders. Now the whole group is calling him king.

They do proclaim it. After laying their garments on the bare steps, the men blow the ram's horn and proclaim, "Jehu is king!" (2 Kings 9:13). Jehu tried to brush the news off, and now it's out for everybody to hear.
